query: Given that refractory high-entropy alloys containing Group IV elements are highly susceptible to embrittlement via oxygen uptake during processing, leading to the precipitation of brittle alpha-HCP phases that raise the transition temperature, how can a powder-based extrusion method be adapted to manage oxygen content during the thermal decomposition of hydride precursors? Specifically, what thermal history and environmental constraints are required to achieve a dense bulk form without catastrophic cracking, and how can the formation of metastable phases be controlled to maximize high-temperature yield strength?

generation.hypothesis: Adapting powder-based extrusion for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Group IV elements requires a two-stage thermal history: (1) a low-temperature, inert-atmosphere decomposition of hydride precursors to release hydrogen and form a clean, oxygen-free powder, followed by (2) rapid consolidation via extrusion under high pressure and moderate temperature to achieve dense bulk forms without catastrophic cracking. Environmental constraints must include ultra-high vacuum or high-purity argon (<1 ppm O2) to prevent oxygen uptake during processing. Metastable phase formation can be controlled by maintaining a valence electron concentration (VEC) < 4.5 to favor a single-phase BCC structure, thereby maximizing high-temperature yield strength while avoiding the precipitation of brittle alpha-HCP phases that raise the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder mixture of refractory high-entropy alloy elements (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W, Ti, Zr) with Group IV elements (Ti, Zr) and hydride precursors (e.g., TiH2, ZrH2) to facilitate hydrogen release and oxygen scavenging.
generation.intervention: Powder-based extrusion method involving thermal decomposition of hydride precursors at 400-600°C under inert atmosphere, followed by extrusion at 800-1000°C under high pressure (500-1000 MPa) to achieve dense bulk forms.
generation.conditions: Ultra-high vacuum or high-purity argon atmosphere (<1 ppm O2), controlled heating/cooling rates to minimize thermal stresses, and extrusion temperatures below the alpha-HCP phase formation threshold.
generation.structural_mediator: Single-phase BCC solid solution stabilized by low valence electron concentration (VEC < 4.5), preventing the precipitation of brittle alpha-HCP phases.
generation.mechanism: Hydride precursors decompose to release hydrogen, which acts as an oxygen scavenger, reducing oxygen uptake during processing. Rapid extrusion under high pressure prevents grain growth and suppresses the nucleation of brittle phases, while the low VEC ensures a ductile BCC structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Dense bulk RHEA with high-temperature yield strength > 400 MPa at 1600°C, room temperature ductility > 10%, and no catastrophic cracking during processing. The material will exhibit a single-phase BCC microstructure with minimal oxygen content (< 500 ppm).
generation.baseline: Conventional powder metallurgy methods (e.g., SPS, arc melting) often result in oxygen contamination, leading to brittle alpha-HCP phase precipitation, increased transition temperatures, and catastrophic cracking during consolidation.
generation.boundary: The method is applicable to RHEAs with Group IV elements (Ti, Zr) and VEC < 4.5. It may not be effective for alloys with higher VEC or those containing elements that form stable oxides at processing temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact decomposition temperature of hydride precursors and the optimal extrusion parameters may vary depending on the specific alloy composition. The long-term stability of the BCC phase at extreme temperatures (>1600°C) requires further validation.
generation.falsification_experiment: Conduct extrusion experiments on RHEAs with Group IV elements under varying oxygen levels (0.1 ppm, 10 ppm, 100 ppm) and measure the resulting microstructure, phase composition, and mechanical properties. If oxygen levels > 10 ppm lead to alpha-HCP phase precipitation and catastrophic cracking, the hypothesis is supported. Conversely, if dense, crack-free bulk forms are achieved even at higher oxygen levels, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . 4.1. Influence of the Milling Time on the Properties of the Powders

The consequences of the variation in the milling time on the properties of the Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr RHEA powder (in stoichiometric ratio) have been assessed by changing the time of milling from 0 h up to 50 h while keeping the rotations per minute constant (250 RPM) under an argon atmosphere.

The XRD results show that after only 1 h of milling, the powders formed four phases: a main BCC1 phase and secondary BCC2, HCP1, and HCP2 phases. The powder microstructures are also significantly altered, as evidenced by SEM and EDS images, even though the segregation of all elements is very pronounced. After milling for 1 h, the Al element was fully dissolved into the other powders, due to higher ductility of its FCC crystal structure compared to the rest of the elements.

By increasing the milling time from 1 to 5 h, the total amount of the secondary phases decreases significantly, thus increasing the main BCC1 fraction.
